content: In 2019, the World Health Organization (WHO) introduced six REPLACE modules, which offer detailed, step-by-step guidance to assist governments in eliminating industrially produced trans-fatty acids (TFA) from the food supply. WHO recommends that countries implement one of two best-practice policies to achieve this goal: either virtually eliminating industrially produced TFA or banning partially hydrogenated oils. Prior to the release of the REPLACE modules, many countries had already removed or were in the process of removing industrially produced TFA from their food supply at national and subnational levels. By September 2022, 60 countries had implemented mandatory TFA limits, with 43 of these adopting best-practice policies that effectively eliminate industrially produced TFA or ban partially hydrogenated oils. This progress demonstrates that reducing global TFA intake is an achievable objective. Providing comprehensive dietary guidance is beyond the scope of these guidelines, as such recommendations should be based on overall dietary goals that account for all necessary nutrients. However, the availability of healthier food options, such as reduced-fat dairy products and lean cuts of meat, is encouraged. The impact of these guidelines can be evaluated by monitoring their adoption and adaptation across countries. At the global level, evaluation will be conducted through the WHO Global database on the Implementation of Nutrition Action (GINA), a centralized platform developed by the WHO Department of Nutrition and Food Safety. GINA shares information on public health nutrition actions implemented worldwide and currently contains data on thousands of policies, laws, and programs from over 190 countries. By providing details on program implementation, country-specific adaptations, and lessons learned, GINA serves as a valuable tool for monitoring and evaluating how WHO nutrition guidelines are translated into policy actions and intervention programs. Future research is needed to address gaps in evidence related to saturated fatty acids (SFA) and TFA. For SFA, research should focus on the health effects of replacing SFA with other macronutrients (e.g., polyunsaturated fatty acids, monounsaturated fatty acids, carbohydrates, or proteins) in diverse populations, particularly in lowand middle-income countries. Studies should also assess the long-term health effects of dietary patterns containing varying amounts of SFA, considering the source (e.g., plant, animal, dairy) and the nature of replacement nutrients or foods. Additionally, research should explore the health effects of SFA intake thresholds lower than 10% of total energy intake in populations with low current SFA consumption, as well as the effects of natural increases in SFA intake in populations with previously low consumption. Genetic and epigenetic factors contributing to individual variations in response to dietary fatty acid changes, particularly regarding LDL cholesterol and cardiovascular disease (CVD) risk markers, should also be investigated. Further exploration of the health effects of individual SFAs is needed to inform dietary guidance. For TFA, research should assess the health effects of TFA intake in children, with long-term follow-up to evaluate impacts on CVD risk and inflammation. Studies should also investigate potential differences in health effects between industrially produced and ruminant TFA, as well as methods to accurately differentiate between these sources. Basic research and epidemiological studies are needed to better understand the physiological pathways through which TFA intake affects mortality and cardiovascular outcomes, including effects on inflammation and immune response. Additionally, current levels of TFA intake in different countries, particularly in developing nations, should be assessed. Research relevant to both SFA and TFA should evaluate the health effects of modifying SFA or TFA intake in individuals at varying risk levels for CVD, including those on lipid-lowering medications. Harmonizing the reporting of CVD endpoints in studies would improve comparability and data synthesis. When assessing lipid endpoints, non-HDL cholesterol and apolipoproteins should be included alongside LDL cholesterol, HDL cholesterol, triglycerides, and other markers. The WHO regularly updates its guidelines to reflect the latest scientific and medical knowledge. This guideline will be reviewed and updated as new data and evidence become available. The WHO Department of Nutrition and Food Safety, in collaboration with other departments within the WHO Secretariat, will coordinate the updating process following formal procedures outlined in the WHO handbook for guideline development. Suggestions for additional questions to address in future updates are welcomed.
